issues.title: Polynomial-time reduction lacks a rational bit-complexity construction

failure_location.quote: $\SV(A,P,Q)$ reduces in polynomial time to $\MA(\wt P,\wt Q)$

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem claims a polynomial-time reduction, whereas its proof only establishes a real-valued equivalence after normalizing by the spectral norm and taking a Cholesky factor. For the rational matrix A=(1,1)^T, the norm is sqrt(2), so the normalized matrix already contains 1/sqrt(2); the old proof gives neither a rational target encoding nor a polynomial bit-size or construction bound. Thus the proof supports the solution correspondence but not the stated discrete polynomial reduction.
issues.overall_effect: The real solution correspondence remains valid, but the polynomial-time clause is unproved and consequently the old proof of NP-hardness of the maximal-angle problem is not established.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the complexity claim for rationally encoded matrices and cone generators, and prove a polynomial-bit rational dilation A = c U^T V with rational c > 0 and rational U,V having orthonormal columns, polynomial dimensions, and polynomial construction time and bit lengths. Mapping the generators through U and V then restores the existing solution correspondence, the polynomial-time reduction, and the NP-hardness corollary.
issues.why_classification: The real-valued Cholesky argument cannot establish a Turing-model polynomial reduction. Repair requires a genuinely new rational construction and bit-complexity analysis, so it is not minor. The construction is nevertheless contained within the reduction subsection, preserves the original isometric-reduction architecture and all affected guarantees, and does not require global reconstruction.

issues.title: Positive-valued local minima need not be Nash pairs

failure_location.quote: Observe also that any solution pair and all local minima of $\SV(A,P,Q)$ are Nash pairs.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Observe that the above means that $u^*$ solves $\SV(A,P,\mathbb R_+ v^*)$ and $v^*$ solves $\SV(A,\R_+ u^*,Q)$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that every local minimum is a Nash pair, meaning it is globally minimizing in each block. What the cone geometry supports is only the corresponding implication for local minima with nonpositive objective value. For example, take P=cone{(1,0),(-1/2,sqrt(3)/2)}, Q=R_+ in one dimension, and A=(sqrt(3)/2,1/2)^T. Writing a unit vector of P as u(theta)=(cos(theta),sin(theta)) for 0<=theta<=2pi/3, the objective is cos(theta-pi/6). The endpoint theta=0 is a positive one-sided local minimum with value sqrt(3)/2, but theta=2pi/3 has value 0, so the pair is not Nash. The omitted sign condition therefore excludes a genuine class of counterexamples.
issues.overall_effect: The old prose overstates the relation between local and blockwise-global optimality. No later formal result identified here relies on the false positive-valued case.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the claim by: every solution pair is a Nash pair, and every local minimum with nonpositive objective value is a Nash pair. The usual normalized conic-interpolation argument can be supplied to justify the latter implication; no assertion should be made for positive-valued local minima.
issues.why_classification: The sign qualification is short and has no downstream formal consequences, but it withdraws the claim for a natural, nondegenerate class of positive-valued local minima, as the counterexample demonstrates. The surviving statement is recognizably comparable and needs no global proof changes, so the loss is limited rather than major, making the issue moderate rather than minor or serious.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Observe also that any solution pair and all local minima with nonpositive values of $\SV(A,P,Q)$ are Nash pairs.

issues.title: The eigenspace projector requires an orthonormal basis

diagnostic_evidence.quote: let $V$ be an orthogonal basis for the image

issues.failure_explanation: The statement allows V to be any orthogonal basis, but the proof treats VV^T as the projector onto Span(V). For an admissible scalar instance G=H=[1] and A=[-1], one has A_x=A_y=-1, lambda=-1, and the relevant eigenspace is E=span{(1,1)^T}, containing the nonnegative eigenvector z=(1/2,1/2)^T. Taking V=(2,2)^T is a valid one-column orthogonal basis of E, but VV^T has eigenvalues 8 and 0, so VV^T z is not z and the stated least-squares test cannot attain zero. Hence item 3 fails under the stated assumption.
issues.overall_effect: The proposition's nonnegative-eigenvector feasibility equivalence is false, and the same projector test in the multiple-eigenspace branch of BFAS can reject a valid support. No later theorem-like result depends on it.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require V to have orthonormal columns in the proposition and in the multiple-eigenspace branch of BFAS, for example by computing a normalized QR basis of the relevant image. Then VV^T is the orthogonal projector and the stated feasibility test is valid.
issues.why_classification: The literal proof makes an invalid projector inference, so this is more than a purely transcriptional typo. However, every relevant image has an orthonormal basis, normalization is immediate and routine, and the correction preserves the proposition, the BFAS test, and all mathematical guarantees without restricting the underlying instances.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: let $V$ be an orthonormal basis for the image

issues.title: Compressed spectral norm requires orthonormal image bases

failure_location.quote: the spectral radius of $A_yA_x$ is $\rho(A_yA_x) = \|U_G^\top AU_H\|^2$

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition permits arbitrary orthogonal bases U_G and U_H but asserts rho(A_y A_x)=||U_G^T A U_H||^2. In the scalar admissible case G=H=A=[1], take U_G=[2] and U_H=[3]. These are orthogonal bases of the required one-dimensional images, while rho(A_y A_x)=1 and the asserted right-hand side is 36. The proof therefore supports the identity only for orthonormal bases.
issues.overall_effect: Item 1 of the proposition is false under its stated basis convention. The other proposition items do not require this particular identity, and no dependent formal result is identified.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Require U_G and U_H to be orthonormal bases of the two images before forming U_G^T A U_H. With that normalization, the compressed spectral-norm identity and item 1 of the proposition hold as proved.
issues.why_classification: The displayed identity is false for the arbitrary scaled bases permitted literally, so a mathematical premise must be corrected. Orthonormalizing the bases is a short, standard, local operation that causes no model restriction, proof reconstruction, or loss of guarantee; hence the issue is minor rather than a typo or a moderate defect.

issues.title: E-AO's sphere updates do not support the claimed convex-subproblem guarantee

failure_location.quote: In our case, the subproblems are convex and the feasible sets are compact, hence AO is guaranteed to have a subsequence converging to a critical pair~\cite{grippo2000convergence}.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the block subproblems are convex and uses that claim to assert subsequential convergence to a critical pair. The actual old display and pseudocode impose P intersect {x:||x||=1}. Even for P=R_+^2, e_1 and e_2 are feasible while their midpoint is not, so this feasible set is nonconvex, including in instances whose global optimum is negative. Thus the specified old method does not satisfy the convexity premise invoked for the stated guarantee; at most it is presented as a heuristic without that justification.
issues.overall_effect: The old source does not establish its stated convex-block convergence justification for E-AO. This does not by itself make the sphere-update procedure undefined or provide a global-optimality issue.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In the negative-optimum regime already isolated by preprocessing, consistently formulate the AO block updates over P and Q intersected with the closed unit balls, not the spheres, and align the pseudocode and output contract accordingly. Initialize from a known negative feasible generator pair so that relevant block optima are nonzero and have active norm constraints. State the cited subsequential criticality guarantee for the resulting ordinary convex-block AO core, while presenting extrapolation as a heuristic overlay unless separately justified.
issues.why_classification: Restoring the convexity premise changes the executable block subproblems and requires checking how ball-constrained accumulation points correspond to critical pairs of the original sphere problem, so it is not a typo or a routine same-algorithm edit. The repair is nevertheless contained, and negative nonzero optima have active norms, so a recognizably comparable AO method and critical-pair guarantee survive without global reconstruction or major mathematical loss.

issues.title: Off-by-one indexing in the circulant-coefficient reconstruction
issues.failure_explanation: For odd n=1+2m, the proof defines the reduced vectors from (a_2,...,a_{m+1}) and (lambda_2,...,lambda_{m+1}). The reconstruction instead labels the recovered entries as a_1,...,a_m and lambda_1,...,lambda_m, then instructs the reader to set a_1=lambda_1=0. This overwrites the first recovered coordinate and leaves the final coefficient a_{m+1}, lambda_{m+1} absent, so the resulting circulant matrices do not implement the proved PSV correspondence.
issues.overall_effect: The unlabelled reconstruction procedure can produce the wrong coefficient arrays, although the preceding formal equivalence lemma uses the correct shifted indices and is not defeated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: For n = 1 + 2m, relabel the recovered coordinates by a_{k+1} = sqrt(2n) x_k and lambda_{k+1} = sqrt(2) y_k for k = 1,...,m, then set a_1 = lambda_1 = 0 and fill the symmetric circulant counterparts. This retains every recovered coordinate and supplies the final indexed coefficients.
issues.why_classification: The preceding equivalence lemma uniquely fixes the one-position index shift, so an informed reader can correct the reconstruction directly without changing any inference, optimization, or formal guarantee. The defect is purely an off-by-one transcription error.
